transcript.text: micrwave keeps tripping the eletric, not every time but like 1 in 3 when i press start, whole kitchen goes off. had to reset the fuse box 4 times today

⚠ Stop using this appliance
Please don't keep resetting the trip. Leave the appliance unplugged and have it checked by a qualified electrician or appliance engineer before using it again. Do not use the microwave again or keep resetting the breaker for it. A trip exactly when Start is pressed points most often to a failing door interlock/monitor switch, with a fault in the high-voltage circuit also possible; either needs a qualified microwave engineer because dangerous stored high voltage can remain inside even when unplugged. The only useful owner check is external: with it unplugged, inspect the door hooks and latch slots for grease, debris, damage or a door that sits out of line. Cleaning accessible debris is fine, but even if it looks normal it still needs professional diagnosis before being used again.

candidates: High-voltage power circuit fault (capacitor, diode, magnetron or inverter) (medium)

reading.symptom: Intermittently trips the electrics when Start is pressed

tags.checkGiven: With it unplugged, look at the plastic hooks on the edge of the door and the slots they click into, and check the door shuts cleanly — food

plan: Safety: a supply trip hazard is active. The fixed safety warning is shown separately, do not repeat it. It must not be used again until a qualified engineer has checked it: say that plainly. You may explain the likely cause and suggest checks that are safe with it switched off and unplugged, but never say or imply that a check could make it safe to use, or that they might not need an engineer.
Checks they have done and what they found: Reset the fuse box 4 times today - The kitchen power had gone off after the microwave tripped it.
The fault they reported is: "Intermittently trips the electrics when Start is pressed". Keep to it: never describe a symptom, result or state they have not told you.
They asked about something unsafe (repeated reset): do not explain how to do it; the fixed safety wording is shown separately. Offer the safe alternative.

Stage 2: the checks they reported did not fix it. Give the next check that best separates the remaining likely causes, or say what the likely faulty part is if the checks already point to one. Until a check has confirmed which part has failed, name it as the likely part and the check that would confirm it; do not tell them to buy, order or replace it.
